top_comments: Everything comes back to whether the demand is really there.Anthropic thinks it is. The got the demand / datacenter match right in Q2, got great margins, and committed hard.They've got:- $114b committed to Google- $110b committed to AWS- $161b committed to Broadcom- $120b committed to SpaceXIf the party continues, they'll go from $50b in revenue to $500b and be fine.But if they don't, it's going to hurt. And that's their only choice, because otherwise, they end up with a frontier model and 50% of the capacity and get eviscerated on either availability or last-minute datacenter leases.It's a big business, but it's not an easy business.

The killer app is AI coding. Claude Code had first mover advantage, was a genuine revolution, and has diffused through the industry with incredible speed. I would imagine most of the huge revenue increase over the last year is due almost entirely to AI coding spend.There are three issues with this. First, the rapid diffusion of the technology means it is very unlikely to continue at the rate of adoption seen over the past year, so it's very hard to extrapolate based on what we've seen so far. Second, many companies are reigning in AI budgets after an initial honeymoon phase. Third, all of the other labs are trying to take a bite of the coding pie, and the price war is already heating up.Add these simple dynamics up and it makes perfect sense why Anthropic would want to IPO now. Things look about as good as they ever will.

articles.title: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
articles.summary: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models

top_comments: I've got a question. I'm having a bit of trouble phrasing it, so please don't assume I'm against learning for learning's sake, that's not the point.Whenever I've tried to learn about LLMs, machine learning, etc. I always come out with a bad feeling, compared to learning about software.Theoretical courses make me feel like it's all baby steps, unless you assume a level of commitment equivalent to a math degree. Practical/applied stuff seems to require levels of compute, training data, etc. that make it unapproachable for a home hacker for everything beyond basic exercises like a handwritten digit classifier.Now this feeling of "impracticality" is perfectly fine. It would be the expected outcome if I was taking a course on classic literature or modern art. But machine learning stuff feels like it could have room for learning-by-doing applications that aren't entirely pointless, so I wonder if there's some way to approach the topic I'm simply not finding.Did anyone have the same experience? any tips if so?

Maybe someone can clarify this:He says:> A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems.But this isn't really true is it? When reasoning models came around with OpenAI's o1, the main feature it had was to be able to try several paths and select the best one. This is what a reasoning model is. This was before agents and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards wasn't it? And then RLVR and agents were added on later. Or am I wrong?

I feel there's a misconception in a lot of the comment threads about what an LLM-from-scratch tutorial is for. Of course you're not going to come out of this kind of tutorial being able to train a useful LLM from scratch. (It requires too much compute, and datasets you don't have access to, and there are a lot of tricks and operational problems to solve for real training runs.) If that's your bar for "impracticality", then sure, this is impractical.But that's not the point; the point is understanding these things better by seeing how they are made (or grown, if you prefer). Building something at a level further down the stack than you will ever go forces you to confront details that shape the layers above that you do deal with. This is one reason why Crafting Interpreters is such a beloved book here on HN.LLMs are now at the core of tools we all use everyday... don't you want to know how they are made? Maybe not everyone has this itch to understand the platforms and tools they use, but I sure do, and it's helped me over and over again. Sure, LLMs aren't like operating systems or compilers. They're a quasi-organic mass of billions of parameters learned during training and honestly nobody (not even the mech interp folks) really deeply understands why they work so well. But that's no reason to completely give up and there is still a lot you can learn.Take RLVR ("Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards"). This is the training technique that made LLMs get so good at programming and math in 2025 and 2026. A lot of people who confidently talk about LLM capabilities either haven't heard of it (and thus end up parroting out-of-date factoids about LLM training derived from the pre-2025 era) or have only a very dim idea of what it is. In this course you actually do RL training of an LLM to get it solving math problems better. You're right down in the details. It's interesting for its own sake but it will also give you a grounding for discussing questions such as: "why did LLM writing get so weird and bad in mid-2026?" and "why is it so hard to train LLMs to be good at things that aren't like math and programming?"Anyway, Sebastian's two books are great and highly recommended; I worked through the first one a year ago and it was one of the best investments of my time in all of 2025. If you prefer video for learning this is great as well (although I'd still say - try the books first).

top_comments: It uses sparseness. I noticed a simple thing way back that for a n-boolean variables, the average size of a satisfiable boolean expression must be 2^n bits - basically every binary number that satisfies it listed out. So if a boolean expression of 4 variables is satisfied by 1111, 1110, and 0000, the number denoting it is 1100000000000001, and for every such number there is a boolean expression of 4 variables and for every expression one number of 16 digits. So it’s a fool’s errand to make a universal solver when average inputs scale at 2^n, if a solution exists it has to leverage the small size of the problems we actually care about, sparsity. Based on the AI description that’s what they did, something with polynomials, but it’s too soon. Looking forward to finding out.

articles.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis Is False [pdf]
articles.summary: See also: Announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50251344

top_comments: While this has no immediate bearing on P-vs-NP, it is interesting to note:- Early CS researchers like Donald Knuth entered CS in the days when regularly someone would come up with a surprising faster algorithm for some problem, and their intuitions were that most problems had faster algorithms than you'd expect.- Later generations of CS researchers, as all the easy algorithms were discovered, and post Karp's definition of NP-completeness (and the Garey & Johnson book, say), began to specialize in proving hardness, and complexity theory with a “zoo” of complexity classes became more about separation and lower bounds, e.g. I've seen algorithms like Arora's PTAS for Euclidean TSP being described as a “failed attempt to prove a lower bound”. So an entire generation of researchers' intuition was mostly in the direction of an elegant universe with neat separation results (even if we couldn't get them).- So e.g. surveys of computer scientists showed most of them believing that P≠NP, and someone like Knuth has always seemed a bit of an outlier for saying that maybe P=NP: his argument was simply that there are so many possible polynomial-time algorithms that we haven't explored, and maybe one of them with a large exponent could solve NP-complete problems. (In response to arguments that many researchers have failed to find any such algorithms, he would say that many researchers have failed to prove that P≠NP.) E.g. in 2017 when Scott Aaronson wrote his survey (https://www.scottaaronson.com/papers/pnp.pdf = https://www.scottaaronson.com/papers/pnp-kindle.pdf) he wrote:> Admittedly, it can be hard to tell whether declarations that P = NP are meant seriously, or are merely attempts to be contrarian. However, we can surely agree with Knuth and Lipton that we’re far from understanding the limits of efficient computation, and that there are further surprises in store.- What we've seen in this month is surprising unexpected algorithms, like o(n log n) algorithms for FFT and integer multiplication, and now this sub–exponential-time algorithm for 3-SAT. (Yes the ETH has had less support than P≠NP but I still gather it's unexpected.)So (though I don't expect intuitions on P≠NP to change, and probably that's still the right intuition… but I'm just an interested amateur), maybe there will be a bit of a swing of the pendulum back to the idea that maybe clever algorithms exist that we just haven't thought of.

This is an amazing and unexpected result. To be clear though, it does not imply that NP is subexponential: "Note that runtime bounds of the form 2^o(n) do not transfer under general polynomial-time reductions (2^n^o(1) would be needed for this), so our result does not imply that general NP problems admit subexponential time algorithms."Edit: To explain more, it is guaranteed that you can reduce any NP problem to 3SAT in polynomial time with a polynomial factor in input size. You still have to solve it.If 3SAT were solvable in polynomial time, then polynomial(polynomial(x)) = polynomial(x) and you're implied to have an overall polynomial time solution.But what we have here is that 3SAT is solveable in subexponential time. subexponential(polynomial(x)) is not guaranteed to be sub-exponential.Further edit: The subexponential solution does carry over to any (?) problems that have can be reduced to 3SAT in a linear number of variables. They list: Counting independent sets, Counting proper q-colorings, Counting perfect matchings.

Wow. Complexity class separations are really really rare.Can an expert in sat solving comment if there's any immediate applications of the method from the paper? Or is SAT solving in general pretty far away from worst-case times, and this is a theoretical algorithm which would be hard to apply in practice.

top_comments: One crucial part of my role as my family's de facto IT support was making sure my mom's FreeCell score record (which was just a Windows registry value) made it from each computer to the next across countless upgrades. She hated the new version that came out somewhere along the way because the card decks changed. (Windows 7? Windows 10? I switched to Linux full time in the XP era so my memory is a little fuzzy.) So I made sure to keep a backup of the Win32 version she was used to, and loaded it onto every machine she ever owned. It wasn't quite the 33 years of its lifetime, but probably close to 30.Mom passed earlier this year, so the FreeCell score record won't ever increment again, but I still made a point to back it up one last time when going through her desktop this summer.

I deplore the day we lost the menu bar and replaced it with "mobile first" designs. The desktop UI was perfected around the time of Windows 95 and has gotten worse with every iteration since then. That, and the increased reliance on non-native frameworks and libraries instead of working with directly with the Windows API in C.

I just resurrected a 90s kids CD-ROM game that shipped for Windows 3.1 - https://github.com/matthewbloch/orlys-draw-a-story-fixesThe finished patch DLL ended up being a tour of the stuff that broke.The game did launch on Windows 11 but the main issue was that the 8-bit pre-DirectDraw behaviour was broken - for 256 colour screens, Windows 11 resolvesld palette indices only once, but the game relies on being able to change the palette for fades etc. Most of the screeen ended up black, but you could see the animated parts just fine.So most of fix ended up being to hook every draw call and implement a virtual GDI that acted like a graphics card of the day.There was a 32-bit disc space check that overflowed, a couple of use-after-free crashes and some racey threading calls that can't have been tested on a machine with 2 CPUs.Backwards compatibility from Microsoft was almost all there, and probably would have kept Orly running for a couple of subsequent Windows releases. But it relies on a developer meeting them half-way, it's not an emulation layer.
